On October 7, 2026, GitHub had two outages of write operations with the same cause, totaling about 19 minutes. The first ran from 15:06 to 15:16 UTC (about 10 minutes) and the second from 16:52 to 17:01 UTC (about 9 minutes). In both windows, actions that save or change data failed across Git operations, pull requests, issues, GitHub Actions, the API, webhooks, sign-in and authentication, GitHub Apps and OAuth, code scanning, Codespaces, and Copilot. Reading data was largely unaffected.

In the first outage, 5.6% of all web and API requests failed, peaking at 8.9%, and more than 12,000 organizations saw failed requests. Up to 26% of Git authentication requests failed, and 17% of Actions workflow runs failed with infrastructure errors. In the second outage, 6.2% of web and API requests failed, peaking at 9.3%, and more than 11,000 organizations were affected. Up to 25% of Git authentication requests failed, and 19% of Actions workflow runs failed. No databases experienced data loss, and operations retried after recovery succeeded.

GitHub relies on an internal service that keeps track of which database servers should receive new and updated data. While replacing machines that run this service as part of regular maintenance, one of the new machines started with an outdated copy of its records, which still listed database servers we had already retired. When this node came online, it incorrectly modified routing configuration with the outdated records, routing write requests to non-existent database servers.

Each outage ended when one of our established machines with correct configuration became the leader of the quorum and sent the correct configuration. After the first outage, we identified the new machine as the source and paused automated maintenance to stop it from being leader again. At 16:52 UTC, an automated maintenance task that did not honor the pause put it back in charge, and the outage happened again. We shut that machine down at 17:02 UTC and have since removed it, and the automation now honors the pause, which was a new regression due to an update of our puppet infrastructure.

To prevent recurrence, we are clearing retired database servers from the service's records before any new machine is added, and we are keeping new machines from being elected leader until their records have been checked. We are also changing our systems to reject configuration that point to servers that don't exist and to keep using the last known-good settings instead. Finally, we are giving responders a faster way to take a misbehaving machine out of service, and adding alerts so changes like this are spotted within seconds.

We will share a more detailed write-up of these incidents in our monthly availability report, along with the status of the repairs we are making to prevent issues like these in the future.

On October 12th 2026 11:51 UTC GitHub experienced elevated 500 responses across several application pages. This caused failures on Issues and Pull Requests as well as Projects and Actions. On October 19, 2026, between 15:24 and 16:52 UTC, GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, and webhooks generated by Actions were degraded. Live updates on GitHub.com and code search were also degraded for part of this time. No data was lost. Impact  - Workflow status updates, logs, and checks were delayed.  - 5.13% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners were delayed in starting, and 0.02% of workflow runs failed.  - During the first 30 minutes, 8.47% of requests to the Actions jobs REST API returned errors. Pages deployments and webhooks generated by Actions runs were delayed. An internal Actions service that stores logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region and immediately retried them from every server at once. The resulting surge of new connections overloaded a shared network link between our data center and that region, which also disrupted other services that use the same link. We mitigated the incident by moving the Actions service off the affected cache servers and reducing connections from other services on the link. We then processed the delayed Actions work. We are continuing to investigate the cause of the initial connection timeouts. We were already in the process of rolling out a limit on how quickly this service can open new connections, but it was still in shadow mode (logging only, not enforcing) at the time of the incident. We have since fully enforced it and capped the service's concurrent connection attempts. We are extending these limits to other Actions services, adding backoff to retries, limiting how much shared network capacity a single service can use, and improving alerting so we can find the source of connection surges faster.

On October 21, 2026, between 13:22 UTC and 19:22 UTC, several GitHub services were delayed due to degradation of our internal event streaming platform. Pull request updates, push webhooks, and push-triggered Actions workflows were delayed by up to 33 minutes until 15:36 UTC. Actions status updates were delayed by up to 33 minutes until 16:16 UTC, holding up some merges and deployments that wait on checks. Webhook deliveries and live updates were delayed by up to 25 minutes until 16:52 UTC. Audit log events were delayed by up to two hours. This was due to servers in the platform running out of memory caused by client reconnections without sufficient retry backoff. We mitigated the incident by moving the busiest workloads to less-loaded servers and adding capacity. We have since added reconnection backoff and added server capacity. We are building a solution for auto-rebalancing connections across servers, and splitting the platform into smaller, isolated clusters to reduce blast radius and time to mitigation of issues like this one in the future.

On October 22, 2026, between 14:55 and 17:28 UTC, search on GitHub.com was degraded. Search-backed features in Issues, Pull Requests, Projects, Actions, Packages, and some REST API endpoints returned errors or incomplete results. On average, 21% of search requests failed, peaking at 52%. Running Actions workflows, uploading and downloading packages, and Git operations were not affected. This was due to the proxies that route requests to our search clusters running out of CPU while setting up encrypted connections. Requests that timed out were retried, which added more load and kept the proxies overloaded. The search clusters themselves remained healthy. We mitigated the incident by adding proxy capacity, after which search recovered at 17:28 UTC. We have started reducing the CPU cost of these encrypted connections. We are also working to make search retries adjustable during an incident without a deployment, and to alert on search failures sooner. Together these will reduce our time to detection and mitigation of issues like this one in the future.

Job status, check run updates, and logs in the GitHub UI and API updated with an average delay of about 2 minutes, and some updates were delayed by up to about 7 minutes.  During this window, a storage dependency that Actions uses to process workflow logs and artifacts throttled our requests. This slowed result processing, causing updates to queue up. incidents.title: Incident with Actions, Issues, API Requests and Pull Requests

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded performance for API Requests, Actions, Issues and Pull Requests
The degradation has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

We saw elevated latency affecting REST API requests, including Checks, and some Actions, Issues, Pull Requests, and GraphQL functionality. Some requests may have been slow or timed out, and notifications were delayed from 17:59 UTC - 18:40 UTC.We mitigated the issue and all services have recovered.

On October 26, 2026, between 17:52 and 18:49 UTC, some customers experienced slower response times across the Checks API, Issues, Pull Requests, GraphQL, Notifications, and related services. Impact was limited to requests served from one of our datacenter sites. Some GraphQL requests failed, and some notifications were delayed. Among GraphQL requests served from the affected site, the average error rate was 5.68%, with a peak five-minute error rate of 14.32%. Unusually large requests for contribution history overwhelmed part of our database infrastructure, causing a backlog. Requests continued reaching the slow component rather than being redirected to healthy systems. Restarting the component restored its performance. The incident was marked mitigated at 18:46 UTC and resolved at 18:57 UTC. We are adding limits to these requests, improving alerts to detect overload sooner, and strengthening automatic redirection to healthy systems.

incidents.title: Disruption with some Copilot services

updates.body: We are investigating reports of impacted performance for some GitHub services.
We are experiencing issues with upstream model providers resulting in a degraded experience across Copilot services. The team is actively investigating the issue.

We are experiencing degraded availability for the GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-6 Luna, and MAI Code 1.1 Flash models in Copilot products and IDE surfaces. This is due to an issue with an upstream model provider. While we work with them to resolve the issue we recommend choosing another model to continue using Copilot.

We are experiencing degraded availability for the GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-6 Luna, and MAI Code 1.1 Flash models in Copilot products and IDE surfaces. We have identified the root cause and working to apply a mitigation. While we work to resolve the issue we recommend choosing another model to continue using Copilot.
We have applied the mitigation and are seeing signs of recovery. We will continue to monitor and expect full resolution soon.
Copilot is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.
The degradation affecting Copilot has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On October 28, 2026, between 13:52 and 15:24 UTC, Copilot users saw errors when using several GPT-family models and the MAI Code 1.1 Flash model. Affected experiences included Copilot Chat in IDEs and on GitHub.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot Code Review, the Copilot Coding Agent, Code Scanning Autofix, and Code Quality. About 9.73% of requests to the affected models failed, with a peak of about 36.97% at the start of the incident.The errors happened because a credential that we use to authenticate with an upstream model provider became invalid. We mitigated the incident by replacing the credential and redeploying the service. We are strengthening how we manage credentials for upstream providers to prevent this type of failure, returning retryable errors when an upstream provider rejects a request, and improving our monitoring so that we detect and mitigate this type of problem faster in the future.

incidents.title: Disruption with Copilot Cloud services

updates.body: We are investigating reports of impacted performance for some GitHub services.

We are experiencing increased failures and latency on our agent sessions service, including creating and listing sessions. This can impact cloud based agent sessions on web, mobile, VS Code, CLI and the GitHub Copilot app.

We continue to experience failure rates of 1-2% and increased latency on our agent sessions service, including creating and listing sessions. This can impact cloud based agent sessions on web, mobile, VS Code, CLI and the GitHub Copilot app.

We continue to experience failure rates of 1-2% and increased latency on our agent sessions service, including creating and listing sessions. This can impact cloud based agent sessions on web, mobile, VS Code, CLI and the GitHub Copilot app. We are actively applying mitigations and monitoring for recovery.
The degradation has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On October 29, 2026, between 05:50 UTC and 12:40 UTC, Copilot agent sessions on GitHub.com and in VS Code were degraded. Live session updates often failed to load, and on average 2.14% of requests to the agent sessions service failed, with a peak of 8.61%. For about 10 minutes around 09:20 UTC, up to 40% of requests to list or create agent sessions failed. Copilot Chat on GitHub.com showed degraded agent session features during this time. The issue occurred when a large increase in task-list requests from a client experiment overloaded the cache that supports the agent sessions service. We mitigated the impact by increasing cache capacity, reducing nonessential load on the cache, and disabling the client experiment. We are moving rate limiting to separate infrastructure, reducing client polling, and improving our alerting so we can detect and respond to this type of overload faster.

updates.body: We are investigating reports of impacted performance for some GitHub services.

A temporarily overloaded component triggered a burst of errors between 14:21 and 14:30 UTC across numerous services. Component health has returned to normal and we continue to monitor while investigating the root cause.
The degradation affecting Pages has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On October 30, 2026, between 14:20 and 14:29 UTC, customers experienced errors across multiple GitHub services. Affected services include Git operations, GraphQL and REST API, Pull Requests, and Issues. At peak, about 3.5% of API requests failed. The incident was caused by slow database requests that held connections open longer than expected, which used all available connections to one of our primary databases. Service recovered at 14:29 UTC once connections were released. Since the incident, we have fixed the code path that held connections open and increased the processing capacity of our database connection layer. We are also improving alerting for this type of overload.

incidents.title: Incident with Actions, Pages, and Webhooks

updates.body: We are investigating reports of degraded performance for Actions and Webhooks
Pages is experiencing degraded performance. We are continuing to investigate.

We continue to investigate delays affecting Actions workflows, Pages deployments, and webhook events, along with errors affecting code search and live updates. We have taken mitigation steps. Actions processing and Pages deployments are showing signs of recovery, but impact has not fully resolved. We are monitoring recovery and investigating the underlying cause.
All affected services have recovered following mitigation. We continue to investigate root cause.
The degradation affecting Actions, Pages and Webhooks has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On October 30, 2026, from 17:50 to 18:32 UTC, Actions, Pages, and Webhooks experienced degraded performance. Actions workflow processing, Pages deployments, and webhook deliveries were delayed, and code search and live updates returned errors. Some Actions queues took additional time to drain after mitigation, and the incident was resolved at 19:23 UTC. The impact was triggered by maintenance on a cloud network gateway connecting an Actions service in the GitHub data center to Redis clusters in the Central US Azure region. The service's Redis client retried aggressively and redialed those connections. That produced a connection storm that saturated the gateway, with about 90% of connection attempts failing. Other services sharing the same network path were degraded as well. We mitigated the incident by removing the affected resources from rotation, which ended the connection storm and allowed the gateway to recover. We have already reduced the number of connection retries in the impacted service and are further improving retry behavior with jittered backoff, shorter connect timeouts, and retry budgets. We are also working with our infrastructure team to make GitHub more resilient to gateway maintenance.

incidents.title: Incident with Dependabot

updates.body: We are investigating reports of impacted performance for some GitHub services.
We are investigating elevated errors when viewing some Dependabot alerts.
We are continuing to investigate elevated errors when viewing some Dependabot alerts. We’ll provide more updates as we learn more.
We have mitigated impact and are seeing recovery. We are monitoring for full recovery.
The degradation has been mitigated. We are monitoring to ensure stability.

On October 30, 2026, between 20:15 and 21:56 UTC, an advisory-publication-driven fan-out caused an unexpected saturation of network connections to the Dependabot alerts datastore. During this period we observed a high rate of write failures on this datastore; users saw elevated failure rates when dismissing or resolving Dependabot alerts, as well as failures when linking Dependabot update pull requests to Dependabot security alerts.  We also observed delays in creating and updating security alerts that extended through November 2, 2026.The unexpected fan-out was caused by a missing job queue throttle after the queues for the fan-out work were migrated as part of system maintenance. We have restored the fan-out throttle and further isolated and throttled these processes to guard against further disruptions.
